title: Large-Language-Model Document Auditors Fabricate Findings at Scale
plain: A study evaluated Google Gemini 3.0 Pro's ability to detect planted contaminants in a constructed corpus of 150 academic papers from supply chain management and medical research, with 450 known contaminants (typographical corruption, semantic reversal, absurd out-of-context insertion) injected across the set. Testing a

angles.claim: Any LLM document-audit pipeline must cap batch size and mechanically re-verify every finding against source text before sign-off.
angles.audience: AI engineering leads governing document-audit or QA pipelines built on LLMs
angles.rank_reason: Directly changes what an engineer configures Monday morning: batch limits and a verification step, both specified in the source's own harness.

angles.claim: An LLM auditor that reports 100% completion at large scale is more dangerous than one that visibly fails, because its errors mimic the target style.
angles.audience: Directors approving AI-based audit or compliance workflows
angles.rank_reason: Gives a director a concrete Thursday question, why does completion rate alone satisfy sign-off, but is a framing of the finding rather than a new operational control.

angles.claim: Detection accuracy on realistic-looking errors is worse than on obviously absurd ones, so audits tuned against toy test cases will pass while missing real contamination.
angles.audience: Engineers designing test suites or acceptance criteria for LLM auditors
angles.rank_reason: Useful for test design but narrower and more inferential than the batch-size and completion-rate claims, since it generalizes a domain-specific accuracy split into a design rule.
